title: Seven Ways to Use Diagnostic Questions to Check for Understanding
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton lays out seven low-tech ways to use a multiple-choice diagnostic question beyond asking which answer is right. His organising mantra is that the thinking does not need to stop with the correct answer. The variations move from answering with and without the options, to explaining why the wrong answers are tempting, to changing the question as little as possible so another option becomes correct. They finish with students generating wrong answers, writing their own diagnostic question, and reverse-engineering a question from its answers. He links several to research on pre-guessing and the Derring Effect, while noting where evidence does not necessarily transfer to maths. Each use is simple enough to run with ABCD cards or mini-whiteboards, so the post works as a menu for a teacher wanting more from each question.
points: The key idea is that a diagnostic question is a springboard: after the correct answer is found, the wrong answers become the material for further thinking.
Asking students to explain why someone might choose a wrong answer, and how to convince them otherwise, tests understanding more deeply than choosing the right option.
'Make the wrong answer correct by changing the question as little as possible' applies the variation-theory principle of changing one element at a time.
Having students generate plausible wrong answers uses the Derring Effect, the finding that deliberately producing errors can aid learning.
Creating or reverse-engineering a question works as an Exit Ticket, homework or assessment because it demands the full depth of understanding.
quotes: This is the obvious one. When presented with a selection of four answers, can students successfully navigate their way past the tempting distractors to arrive at the correct answer?

A 2023 paper by van den Broek suggests that asking students to guess the answer before showing them the options improves memory and recall. The participants in the study were challenged to translate words, so there is no guarantee that the same effect transfers to mathematics or any other domain, but it is worth a go.

I have a mantra when it comes to diagnostic questions: the thinking doesn’t need to stop with the correct answer. Sure, students may be able to explain why B is the correct answer. But can they explain why someone else might think D is the correct answer?

This time the challenge is to change the question as little as possible to make one of the incorrect answers correct. As little as possible is the key. It taps into one of the key principles of variation theory, changing one key element, holding everything else the same, and observing the impact it has on the solution.

So, we can present students with the question without the four possible answers and ask students to generate plausible wrong answers for the question (alongside the correct answer). Students can swap answers with their partners and explain their reasoning. And then the big reveal can come when we show students what the original choice of answers is.

This is a step up from the previous option as this time students need to generate a question as well as the correct answer, plausible wrong answers, and reasons for those answers. This makes a fantastic Exit Ticket, homework assignment, or assessment question, allowing students to demonstrate the depth of their understanding.

You tell students the topic - in this case mental addition - show them the four answers, indicate the correct one, and challenge them to think what the original question was. Again, they can swap ideas and justifications with their partner before the big reveal.
